title: Protect the aggregate when two commands race
description: Both handlers read the same stream revision. Change the append contract to see which events enter history, whether the aggregate invariant survives, and why conflict handling belongs in the domain.

strategies.label: Append without an expected revision
strategies.detail: Accept both event batches even though each decision used stale state.
strategies.rule: The store appends whenever the stream exists. It does not prove that the command was evaluated against the latest aggregate state.

strategies.label: Require the loaded revision
strategies.detail: Append only while the stream still matches the revision the handler read.
strategies.rule: The first append moves the stream forward. A second append that still expects the old revision fails atomically and must not be treated as success.

strategies.label: Reload and re-evaluate
strategies.detail: After a conflict, rebuild current state and run the business rule again.
strategies.rule: A conflict triggers a fresh decision, not a blind append retry. The domain can now accept, reject, or ask a person to resolve intent.

scenarios.label: Two customers reserve the last seat
scenarios.detail: The aggregate has one seat left. Two command handlers independently observe the same remaining capacity.

appends.detail: The first reservation enters the stream.
The stale decision also enters the stream because no revision was checked.

append-any.summary: Replaying both validly stored facts oversells the show. An append-only log faithfully preserves a bad decision; immutability does not create correctness.
append-any.nextStep: Compensate one reservation, notify the affected customer, and require expected-revision appends for this aggregate boundary.

appends.detail: The stream still matches v12, so the event is appended atomically.
The stream is now v13, so an append that expects v12 is rejected.

expected-revision.summary: The event store protects the per-stream compare-and-append boundary. The rejected command has not yet been evaluated against the new state.
expected-revision.nextStep: Reload v13 and run the reservation rule again. Return a domain result such as sold out instead of exposing a storage conflict as the final user message.

appends.detail: Customer A reserves the final seat.
After replaying v13, the aggregate sees zero capacity and emits no event.

reload-recheck.summary: Re-evaluation converts a low-level conflict into the correct business outcome. No blind retry can oversell the aggregate.
reload-recheck.nextStep: Return a sold-out response with the current aggregate version. Retry only if the domain rule still permits the command after reload.

scenarios.label: Two devices add different cart items
scenarios.detail: Two commands touch the same cart stream but represent compatible intent after the aggregate is reloaded.

appends.detail: The mouse is also recorded without checking the state used for its decision.

append-any.summary: This final state happens to be acceptable, but the write path skipped the aggregate's concurrency boundary. A different pair of commands could violate a quantity or inventory rule.
append-any.nextStep: Do not infer that append-any is safe from one friendly race. Use expected revisions consistently, then make retry behavior explicit per command.

appends.detail: The first compatible intent is recorded.
The second command still expects v3 and must be evaluated again.

expected-revision.summary: The concurrency check preserves the aggregate boundary, but conflict rejection alone does not complete a compatible user action.
expected-revision.nextStep: Reload v4, verify that adding the mouse remains allowed, then append it using expected revision v4.

appends.detail: The keyboard enters the stream first.
After reload, the mouse still satisfies quantity and inventory rules.

reload-recheck.summary: A bounded re-evaluation safely keeps both compatible intents. The second append uses the newly observed stream revision.
reload-recheck.nextStep: Cap retries, preserve the command ID for idempotency, and return the final revision so the client can request read-your-write behavior.

scenarios.label: Two devices replace the shipping address
scenarios.detail: Both updates are individually valid, but software cannot infer which conflicting user intent should win.

appends.detail: Berlin silently replaces the first intent during replay.

append-any.summary: The state is structurally valid, but arrival order silently decides between contradictory intentions. The business meaning is unresolved.
append-any.nextStep: Surface a conflict to the user or define an explicit domain policy. Do not let storage arrival order masquerade as business intent.

appends.detail: Paris is recorded against the state the handler loaded.
The Berlin command cannot append against stale revision v8.

expected-revision.summary: The store prevents a silent lost update. The second user's intent still needs an explicit resolution.
expected-revision.nextStep: Return the new address and revision to the second client, then let the user confirm whether Berlin should replace Paris.

appends.detail: Reload reveals a competing change, so the handler refuses to guess which intent wins.

reload-recheck.finalState: Shipping address is Paris; review requested
reload-recheck.summary: Re-evaluation does not mean automatic retry. For contradictory intent, the safe domain decision is to stop and ask.
reload-recheck.nextStep: Expose both values with the current revision. Append a new address-change event only after the user confirms the intended destination.
